title: How long is each part of a folded paper strip?
description: A paper strip one unit long is folded into two equal parts and opened again. The crease splits the unit into two equal lengths, and each length is named. Keeko's doubt, that each part is two units long because there are two parts, is broken.
teaching_notes: One idea: folding a one unit strip into two equal parts makes each part a fractional unit of the strip. Watch for students who read the number of parts as the length of each part.

source: Take a strip of paper. We consider this paper strip to be one unit long. Fold the strip into two equal parts and then open up the strip again. Taking the strip to be one unit in length, what are the lengths of the two new parts of the strip created by the crease?
video_script.why: The child folds a one unit strip into two equal parts and names the length of each part, the same way a roti is shared between two children.
video_script.substitution: Treat the paper strip as the roti and the crease as the cut that shares it between two children.
video_script.anchor: A paper strip one unit long, folded in the middle so its two ends meet, and opened again
video_script.wrong_answer: each part is two units long because there are two parts
video_script.wrong_move: Keeko says each part is two units long because there are two parts. Two parts of two units would make four units, but the whole strip is only one unit, so the bubble is struck.
video_script.payoff_line: Each part is one half of a unit long

final_answer.spoken: each part is one half of a unit long

never_show: 2 units as the length of one part
maths_rules: one fold with the ends meeting makes 2 equal parts
1 unit shared into 2 equal parts: each part is 1/2 unit
slip: 2 units for each part would make the 2 parts 4 units together, but the strip is 1 unit
video_script.design: One idea: one unit folded into two equal parts gives each part one half of a unit. Assumes equal sharing of a roti. Wrong idea: the number of parts is the length of each part. The strip stays on the board to the end.

narration: <bookmark mark='book'/>This is a question from your book about a strip of paper.
<bookmark mark='strip'/>The paper strip is one unit long.
<bookmark mark='fold'/>We fold it into two equal parts and open it again. The crease splits the strip.
<bookmark mark='ask'/>How long is each of the two parts?

narration: <bookmark mark='unit'/>The strip is the whole, as the roti was the whole.
<bookmark mark='roti'/>When a whole is shared between two children, the two shares are equal.

narration: <bookmark mark='fold'/>Step one, fold the strip so that its two ends meet.
<bookmark mark='open'/>When we open it, the crease makes two equal parts. The two parts lie exactly on top of each other.

beats.on_screen: Step 2: 1 unit is shared into 2 equal parts; each part is one of the 2 equal parts

narration: <bookmark mark='share'/>Step two, think of the strip as one unit shared into two equal parts. Do it the same way as the roti.

beats.on_screen: Answer: each part is 1/2 unit long
narration: <bookmark mark='ans'/>Each part is one half of a unit long. Both parts have the same length.

beats.on_screen: Keeko with a raised hand beside the boxed answer
narration: <bookmark mark='hand'/>Keeko has raised a hand. Let us check the doubt and solve it.

beats.on_screen: Keeko's doubt in a bubble; two long parts are laid end to end and stretch far beyond the strip; the bubble is struck through

marks.fix: two parts of that size are laid end to end and stretch far beyond the strip, and the bubble is struck through
marks.count: the words how many parts are crossed out and the words how long is each part are circled

narration: <bookmark mark='doubt'/>Keeko thinks each part is two units long because there are two parts.
<bookmark mark='fix'/>But two parts of two units each would make four units. The whole strip is only one unit.
<bookmark mark='count'/>The number of parts tells us how many pieces there are, not how long each piece is.
